en: The Determination of Śambhu (p. 77).
Auspiciousness.
* * * * * * * * * * * * * The Sādhana.
Since, by bowing to that immutable Śambhu, I shall become the daughter of Himavat;
O Lord of the World, I ask you for this concise method of accomplishment out of fear of Vyāsa.

Having placed within your own heart the worship of the glorious Śiva-nature, which grants all desires of the mind, make it abide amidst your internal transformations. May we hold you in our hearts; may divine perfections be yours.
First, by all means, prevent Śakti from entering living beings;
then, having performed this, perform the worship of the deity for the sake of attaining all perfections.
Having received initiation according to the three commands, either from a guru or from oneself...
Thereafter, one should perform the rite of self-consecration along with one's consort.
Having assumed the lotus posture (saroruhāsana) and bathed before him like a planet in the sky,
one should reach a secluded place and worship the glorious Supreme Lord (Śrī Parameśvara).

Having touched the supreme abode, he who possesses the sovereign light should offer a flower along with its cause; he shall liberate that which is to be enjoyed by him. The vessel containing water for the *arghya* offering, together with the offered flower and its cause—this is the [proper] vessel.
With the casting of the glance accompanied by the mantra, one should partake of the threefold *śānti* offering (*bali*) with the detached syllables of the *alī*,
which destroy all obstacles.
Having meditated upon [the deity] who bestows all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi), surrounded by the spirits (bhūta) and others, one should recite:
*oṃ hrīṃ sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyo hrūṃ svāhā*.
Then, one should fashion a square protective enclosure (laṃ) in front of oneself, as wide as the arms.
One should place the *smara-cchokā* [mantra] three times upon that [tablet], such as a golden plate;
one should fashion the *saṃvartikā* [folded paper] upon golden plates and the like for the nine-fold worship.
These nine abodes, smeared with rice-water, consist of fragrance, the moon, and the sun.
The base, however, should measure one-fourth [of the height] for the purpose of support;
it belongs to the primary pedestal (*nidāna*) together with its receptacle, which bestows the presence of the deity.
It should be situated outside the four-finger width from the principal forehead-region.
One should fashion a staff-like ornament measuring four finger-breadths for the worship of Bāṣpa;
likewise, it should be so for the purpose of worshipping the five Śrī-gurus who enjoy the realms beginning with Saṃvarta, within the portion of Candra.
After that measurement, one should subsequently decorate [the area] with those [elements] previously mentioned,
for the purpose of worshipping the *pīṭha* with the mantras prescribed for the principal [deity], along with their underlying rationale.
Once the perimeter of the maṇḍala has been prepared, one should commence the worship according to the rationale (*hetu*).

For the purification of one who has dwelt in the abode of cattle, for the sake of immortality, and for the sake of [attaining] nectar—O Pārvatī, there are exactly five: the *ṇi* group, the self, mortals, the netherworld, and the *nāgas*.
The jewels consist of the first, middle, and final parts of *keśa*, *soma*, and *yama*.
One should worship Umā with the seed-syllables joined by *śiva*, *bhṛgu*, *kāla*, *ratna*, and *meṣa*,
and with the earth (*dharā*) and the sixth vowel, placed at the beginning and end of the five verses.
Then, having placed it above that in the arghya vessel, one should worship according to the prescribed rite. Then, by means of the Goddess’s [mantra], [one should offer] once, and then three times.
For this reason, it brings about the destruction of all sins.
One should satisfy the world with that which bestows the body that grants the accomplishment of all commands.
Having sprinkled the "flower" of all limbs, which is adorned by the arrival of all mandalas, one should practice the nyāsas of the hands, body, and mouth, which arise from the ninefold entry.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, on the leaf that bestows the attainment of the five groups, the mandala for worship has been completed; may you possess divine accomplishments. Thus ends the first section.
I speak of that Śrī Parameśvara, by propitiating whom Dhātṛ creates, Keśava protects the world, and Rudra withdraws it at the time of dissolution;
indeed, Śrī Parameśvara himself creates, protects, and destroys.
Listen to [the teaching on] Sarveśvara, who has cast down even the three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
Therefore, by performing this practice, the practitioner certainly attains the five cities; there is no doubt regarding this, for it occurs even without the triad and so forth.
One should place eight [deities] together: Ambā, Bhṛgu, Kaṣāyamā, Pūtanā, Vajriṇī, Pālā, and Sarpā; these are my excretions.
One should add this to the zodiacal sign by means of the vital points, the moon, the sun, and fire.

This twelve-fold soul, the lord of consciousness at birth, bestows the experience of what has been experienced. One should meditate upon the peak-syllable, resembling the morning sun, within the lotus of the heart.
One should attain oneness with that [deity] through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) which has assumed its form.
One should deposit the *kūṭa* [mantra] in its limbs by means of the [deities] joined [with them]; listen to the sixfold sequence:
[the deities are] Nanta, Mūrtti, Marma, Bhauta, Nātha, Sena, and Triviṣṭapa.

(With the little finger, ring finger, middle finger, index finger, and thumb—known as the "increasing" sequence—at the palate,) one should divide [the breath] with the fingers thus: three, two, one, ten, and three.
And [one should visualize] faces facing west, north, south, east, upward, and downward.
In the houses of the Cora, Kūpa, Pārada, Śrutimukha, Cūḍa, and Veśman [groups],

one should again meditate upon the Lord as a mass [of light]. Having thus formed the connection, one should worship the door-keepers— those who destroy all obstacles, such as the Vidyut-praghna and Gṛhatāta.
One should meditate upon [the deity] who holds a white lotus resting on the moon, and a trident, sword, and the gesture of threatening (*tarjanī*) in his right hands, which destroys all obstacles.
His seed-syllable (*bīja*) consists of the letters *ka*, *i*, *śva*, *ra*, *a*, *m*, *bu*, *sa*, *vi*, *t*, *rī*, *so*, *ma*, *ā*, *rya*, *ma*, *ra*, *va*, *ra*.
In the name [of the deity], from the pair of seeds at the beginning and end of the fourth offering and so forth—
one should thus worship the red [deity] who illuminates the day, white and situated on the right;
[this is] the *śambara* of his mandala, which effects the grace of the Mother.
One should worship the yellow [deity] in this manner in Aries; hear now its garment:
it consists of the circles of Īśa, Saṃvarta, and Sāvitrī, along with the two lines.
One should honor the gatekeepers three times by name,
preceded by the offering of incense, unbroken rice, lamps, mudrās, and oblations. Immediately thereafter, one should [worship] in the seat of mantras (mantrapīṭha), beginning with those deities.
One should perform worship according to the divisions of the ends of liquor, and according to the fivefold division.
Having recited the long mantra of the nine mudrās and garments,
one should perform worship with handfuls of fragrant flowers and [proceed] as follows.
Then, one should worship the Gurus, the beginningless Lords of Kula (the inconceivable friends),
according to the divisions from the base to the head, and should offer incense and other articles with verses.
(Then, the one who has conquered the senses [should proceed] to the worship of the remaining lords of the gods.)
One should practice that which initiates [the rite] for the sake of attaining all merit collectively.
Immediately after the *meda* [mudrā], having bound the *kamaṭhī* [mudrā] once toward the sky,
one should recollect the *ekāṅgasaṃsthāna* [mudrā] and meditate upon the lotus.
[One should worship] the head [of the deity] with red pearls, [and] the hands with released power (mukta-śakti).
Indeed, one should satisfy the Mother with the forms [of the deities] and likewise with the mantras beginning with Candra.
Having meditated upon the lotus at his navel and head, one should remember the elemental space (bhautaka-kha).
Having worshipped him, one should then meditate upon the form of the Lord that arose from the crest of the atom—
[the forms] of the cloud, the breast, the great sun, the book, and the linga [within the self], respectively.
Through the increase of the fruit of worship, the result [is attained] as in the case of the *Purāṇas* and other [scriptures].
In the Śambara [tantra], the ritual should be performed with *śambaras*; in the Vedas, with flowers and the like;
at the end, with those belonging to the group beginning with women; and in between, with lotuses (*kajā*).
[This concludes] the determination by the venerable Śambhu regarding those who sleep in their father’s house and so forth,
those who dwell in [other] houses, and the constant [application of] the signs of the Āgamas;
it bestows the attainment of the five groups in the Parṇa [chapter].
May the divine perfections be the synonyms for your worship of Gaṅgā.
The second section.
Now, listen to the sovereignty over the world of the immortals...
For the sake of attaining the group of five,
one should form the "peak" (*kūṭa*) with a single finger on both palms.
[This applies] to the names of the Elder, the Threatening Finger, the Others, the Akaniṣṭha, and the Crotch.

With two [lines], one should mark the vital points (*marmas*) and *bindus* starting from the forehead down to the path [of the eyebrows] in the eyes and other areas; likewise, one should observe those of the face:
a white [dot] at the nostril, a red [dot] on the forehead, a garland [of dots] on the mouth, and a garland on the neck.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters of the *kūṭa* mantra in sequence with their respective colors: yellow in the heart, dark blue in the *kṣaya* [the throat], smoky grey in the anus, and the color of the sun (yellow) in the feet. One should place it on all limbs;
starting from the entire body and ending at the aperture of the crown, one should do this for the sake of attaining stability of the body.
Then, with the six previously mentioned [syllables] and the three bodily *kūṭas* that bestow the body,
one should perform [the rite]; thereafter, one should worship the God who has reached the further shore of sound and is beyond the ritual injunctions.

Having restrained the senses from their objects, one should meditate in sequence upon the white, red, and black peaks [of the breath] within the moon, sun, fire, and wind; likewise, at the throat and the mouth,
one should contemplate that mass with a crest of the aforementioned colors, its body entwined with a garland of lotus fibers.
Having performed the raising of Kuṇḍalinī, one should cause her to descend into the lotus-bud.
At the mere moment of that descent, the form of the venerable Navātman— remover of the suffering of men and bestower of liberation while living— should be meditated upon with a mind fixed upon it.
Having the form of a fresh rain-cloud, dancing and endowed with youth,
her lotus-like big toe of the left foot rests upon her right thigh in the *argha-paryaṅka* posture;
she possesses a great conch and a jeweled discus, and her skin has the appearance of a white lotus.
With a waist like a sword-blade or a firebrand, adorned with human skulls,
having five faces and three eyes, with coarse hair standing erect on her head,
she bears the hand, trident, discus, and other banners of the Creator.
With her left hands, she holds the weapons of Śambhu for the liberation of the world;
with her right, she holds a *pāribhadra* flower perfumed by the scent of Brahmā’s feet, a book for recitation, and the destruction of fear; her face is ever smiling.
Enveloped by messengers with palms joined in reverence within the cremation ground,
omniscience proceeds from the worship of the trident performed by the sacrificer;
as long as the illusion arising from the three times persists, it proceeds from the worship of the wheel.
Through the worship of the banner, O Śivā, one attains travel to the fourteen worlds;
through the worship of the book, one gains mastery over the Vedas and other scriptures.
Through the worship of Abhayā, the fear of the six realms of existence will certainly perish;
through the worship of Vidhikarā, there shall be the destruction of obstacles from above;
and through the worship of her feet, the destruction of obstacles that move downward occurs.

The mantras beginning with Ambā and ending with Kūrā have been proclaimed for the purpose of consecrating the weapons; make them endowed with nine dots (bindus). Thus, having recited the root mantra and established the regulation of the vital breaths (prāṇa), [proceed].
Having formed a handful of flowers together with unbroken rice grains and fragrant substances in three parts,
and having offered the vessel of *arghya*, one should enter [the mandala] for the sake of purification.
In the midst of that, O Dear One, [one should place] a white [substance] smeared with fragrant water.
One should present perfumes, incense, lamps, food offerings, and fruits;
and having displayed conch shells filled with fragrant water, chowries, and mirrors, one should offer white dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains of rice.
Having meditated on the three atoms at the crown of the head, one should divide them into three parts.
Then, for the sake of the world’s activity, his vital breaths become the Śaktis and Bhairavas;
I shall speak of them, so listen, O Mistress of Śakti!

In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, in the chapter [dealing with] the attainment of the five groups, the ninth worship of Śakti has been completed; may you possess divine perfections (*divyasiddhi*). The Third Section.
The gods are the cause and the task, while the gods are considered the means;
for the sake of accomplishing the people’s welfare, the people are the task, and the gods are the sole means to achieve that end.
The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) may be either sequential or simultaneous.
Therefore, O Goddess, impelled by worship, meditation, recitation, and so forth in sequence,
one should worship Maṅgala and Carcaka, beginning with Mṛḍa and ending with Antaka.
Yoga, Harasiddha, Bhaṭṭa, and the one called Kilikila; Kālarātra, Bhīṣaṇa, and Kārdhaśūlavidhāraka;
Kucacibukahasta—this group of eight is red in color.
In this enclosure, one should worship in sequence Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kumārikā, Vaiṣṇavī, Ghoṇikā, Śākrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Kamalā.
Having formed these nine [deities] as distinct from the seed-syllables, one should worship them.
One should worship the gods with those *kūṭa* mantras ending in a nasal (*anusvāra*), joined with the secret powers (*guhyaśakti*). One should perform the worship with those *kūṭa* mantras;
at the end of these, one should offer [the goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī, and then present incense and the other offerings.
One should display the *yonimudrā* to the deity; then, having performed the worship three times again, one should offer incense accompanied by the sounding of the bell.
Thereafter, as before, one should worship the heart and other limbs with the nine *kūṭa*-mantras consisting of the *rasas*.
Then, having made a formal petition, one should perform the worship of the limbs of enjoyment on the exterior:

in the southeast (Jātavedas), the northeast (Bhūteśa), the southwest (Yātudhāna), and the northwest (Samīraṇa), as well as in the ninth direction (above) and the four cardinal directions, one should [worship] the heart and the other [limbs] in sequence with the [respective mantras].
Having satisfied Devavrata with the [appropriate] cause and having shown the one named Yoni, one should then perform a hundred recitations for the New Mistress.
The recitation for each of the heart-mantras and the others is prescribed as ten [times] each.
Then, having performed circumambulation and prostration, one should recite the hymn nine times:
Oṃ, salutations to the one whose nature is born from the power of Druhiṇa and Vaikuṇṭha.
Salutation to the one who dwells in the *bindu* at the throat of the *ādhāra*,
whose radiant body moves through the sixteen divine cavities (*bila*) within,
and who destroys the karma of birth, enjoyment, dissolution, disease, and suffering.
To the one who possesses the knowledge that narrates the world known as past, present, and future;
to the destroyer of the six waves of existence; to the annihilator of those who propound the voidness of being;
to the one whose very self is the destruction of the fear of the world terrified by the dread of the six states of rebirth.
To the one who brings about the repeated destruction of worldly existence and its exhaustion;
to the singular embodiment that destroys wrinkles and grey hair; to the bestower of nectar;
to the one who grants liberation while living, endowed with the recollection of all [past] ignorance.
This supreme secret hymn, consisting of five verses, is purifying;
a lord of men should recite it daily for the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation,
for the completion of worship, for the accomplishment of all atomic powers (*siddhis*), and for liberation and happiness.
At the end of this, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the *nau* mantra for the sake of attaining the three commands.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, it is said that [this] bestows the attainment of the five groups on the leaf.
O worthy one, may all perfections be yours; the worship of the messenger is now concluded.
The Fourth Section.
Śrī.

"Having bowed to that imperishable Śambhu— the Lord of Svārājya, Hāṭaka, and Īśāna, who is the means for attaining liberation while living— I, the daughter of Himavat, shall speak. O Lord of the World, out of fear of [prolixity], I ask you about a concise method of practice."
Having placed within my heart the worship of the glorious Śiva-natured Self— which grants the fulfillment of every desire— may your divine perfections abide ever anew within my heart.
First, let us by all means effect the entry of Śakti into living beings. Setting aside [other matters], perform the worship of the Deity for the sake of attaining all perfections.
Having received from the Guru, or by oneself, the initiation (dīkṣā) proclaimed in the three commands (ājñās),...
Then, having performed the consecration together with his wife according to the ritual procedure,
and having completed the preliminary bath and other bodily preparations,
he should go to a secluded place and worship the Lord Śrīpameśvara.
Having recollected the supreme abode, that other light which is the Lord’s sovereignty,
one should offer a flower with its stalk; by that, one should liberate [the soul] within the object of enjoyment.
One should offer the *śānti-bali* in three ways with the vessel containing half-food, water, a cause (or reason), and offered flowers,
using the detached *alivarṇa* mantra which destroys all obstacles.
Having meditated on [the deity] who bestows all accomplishments, surrounded by the spirits (*bhūta*) and others, one should recite:
*Oṃ hrīṃ sarvakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyo hrūṃ svāhā*.
Thereafter, one should fashion a square sacrificial altar (*puroḷa*) before oneself...
One should place three verses upon a golden plate or similar surface within that [mandala].
In the ritual of the ninefold worship, one should prepare a rolled scroll (*saṃvarttikā*) on a golden plate or the like,
using ink made from gold and a vessel of gold, upon a surface smeared with rice flour and white sandalwood paste.

The base (alāghu), however, should measure one-fourth [of the height] for the purpose of installation; it bestows [merit] upon the primary donor who is the cause of the [temple] dedicated to Sārpātri. It should be placed at the principal location of the forehead, four finger-breadths outside [the central axis].
For the worship of Bāṣpa, one should fashion [the vessel] resembling a staff, measuring four finger-breadths;
likewise, for the purpose of sacrifice, its petal should be in the portion of the moon.
[This applies to] the five illustrious Gurus who enjoy the realms of Saṃvarta and the others.
One should subsequently adorn [the area] from above and behind with those [offerings] mentioned previously,
for the sake of the valid reason of performing the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) by means of the principal mantra.
At the conclusion of the prepared maṇḍala, one should begin the worship based on the causal principle (*hetuyajana*).
For the purification of impurities contracted while dwelling in the abode of cattle, and for the sake of immortality,
fire alone is clearly the innate form of Śambhu, who consists of the ninefold self.

Listen to [the practice] external, internal, and external, for the attainment of all fruits. Having churned [the elements], like the fire that has arisen within the wood, or like Agni Dhanañjaya, take that [fire] and, by means of your own Vaidvata fire, make it threefold.
One should cast the mortar into that Veda-triangle, which has a single neck with a hollow of seventeen finger-breadths and a rim of twelve finger-breadths;
or else, when such a circle is ablaze and honored in three ways.
When it has been honored in five ways with streams of clarified butter by the nine *kaṇus*,
one should offer flowers mixed with milk, sap, honey, and sugar, according to one's capacity.
Or, one may offer only sesame seeds with clarified butter, measured by the footprint of a sparrow,
a hundred times, together with the deity Śambarasvāmin in his embodied form. Ten flowers each are prescribed for the heart-mantra and the other limbs.
Even in the case of daily rites, for the sake of accomplishment, there is an oblation [of a portion of the mantra];
[there are] mudrās; [and] the bow [is placed] on the forehead. With the weapon-mantra, the dismissal of the new lord is performed three times twice.

In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, on the leaf [dealing with] the bestowal of the attainment of the five groups: "The fire-oblation has gone to the non-Lord; may you possess divine perfections. The Fifth Section.
The Sixth Section.
O Lord, if one does not perform the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times before the Guru.

Likewise, for the removal of the *anusvāra*, one should resort to the *sāpana* rite. Having conquered the diseases of the chest by means of recitation (*japa*), one should perform meditation (*dhyāna*) which bestows a subtle body.
For fevers and other ailments, one should employ the words of Śrī Śambhu accompanied by fire-offerings (*homa*).
The sequence of fevers arising from phlegm, bile, fire, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and dual combinations [of these] is as follows:
upon seeing the new Lord [Viṣṇu], one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times and perform a hundred *homa* offerings.
One should offer a hundred handfuls of white mustard seeds together with neem leaves.
One should destroy all fever that is difficult to eradicate; therefore, there is no delusion here.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should offer ten thousand oblations of air into the fire at the time of the Upakāla, which has surpassed the cities with its vast shadows and is auspicious.
Having seen hemorrhoids that are difficult to conquer, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times;
for their pacification, one should offer a thousand fruits of the *vilva* tree as oblation.
Having seen the five types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) causing affliction, one should recite it thirty thousand times.

One should offer thousands of *kadamba* fruits as oblations to Śiva. Upon seeing epilepsy (*apasmāra*), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. For the sake of pacification, one should offer ten thousand oblations of the flesh of a black dog into the sacrificial fire.
Seeing one afflicted by urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), one should recite the mantra of Śiva fifty thousand times;
for the sake of pacification, one should offer a thousand *jambū* fruits into the fire.
Seeing one afflicted by difficult-to-conquer vomiting (*chardi*), one should recite it one hundred thousand times and likewise perform the fire-oblation.
A leaf marked with a black dog [is used] for the destruction of bodily diseases. Having seen one with various great white spots, one should recite the name of Śiva one hundred thousand times.
One should offer oblations of udumbara wood mixed with ghee for the pacification of leprosy.
Upon seeing hiccup, asthma, or jaundice, one should recite the mantra sufficiently;
furthermore, for the sake of pacification, one should offer ten thousand handfuls of peas as oblations.

Having seen the onset of diseases such as severe wind-disorders, blood-bile disorders, urinary ailments, abdominal enlargements, growths, great calamities, insanity, erysipelas, swellings, and jaundice, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer oblations of *dūrvā* grass to Śiva.
Having seen the flower, one should offer ten thousand oblations to Raktavedhas.
Having previously consecrated ten thousand [oblations] for Viśvatāta Navātman,
thereupon happiness arises and diseases are destroyed.
There are ten million varieties of diseases, one for each [organ];
to destroy them, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with water enriched by nails, hair, and fat.
Thereupon, all diseases having departed, the body becomes pure in form.
One should undertake the boat-like meditation for the sake of renewing the body;
it bestows the attainment of the five groups according to the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya* leaf.
May the collection of diseases depart—may you possess the divine... [omitted].
Sixth Section:
One should meditate on the group of nine and the group of five at the golden abode, which is the attainment of the *tāla* measure.
Listen to the number of groups [of letters] ending with the *bindu* and reaching as far as the *prāṇa*.
The Lord of Yogins, the Year, destroys the strength and the joy of the enemy;
he attains greatness, bestowing upon Indra the attainment of supreme power and vigor.
By practicing for a year with these qualities, the yogi becomes a vajra-body, a lord of the earth;
through the contraction of the sun [of passion], that man shall become equal to Śakra.
Below that, one should meditate on the small [channel] situated in the middle of the snowy night-lotus.
The *pada* together with the nasal drop (*bindu*) destroys wrinkles and graying hair within a year.
Freed from all states of existence and adorned with the qualities of omniscience, the yogi arises after three years; he rejoices in the sun and delights in the moon.
The Lord, who has abandoned all vows [of worldly life],
who is filled with the qualities of omniscience, and who is the sovereign in the city of Dhanañjaya,
caused the ocean of the hearts of his horses to flow with inexhaustible nectar.
Endowed with the aforementioned qualities, he rejoices in the world of Vāyu.
One should meditate on the primary principle (pradhāna) for one year during the state of purity;
endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, he rejoices in the world of Śiva.
In the bile [element], one should meditate on the pair of Śambhus, who have reached the bow of Muditā;
from that, one becomes omniscient. In the city of the dissolution, one should meditate on the all-pervading Lord as the fourth, adorned by that very same [state].
From the month of Rasa [Mārgaśīrṣa], the yogas are produced, numbering as many as the elapsed [months] plus the number of Jupiter's revolutions;
one should always meditate on that third [yoga] in the wind, conjoined with Rudra.
After three years, one truly attains the status of a Lord of all worlds.
One should meditate on her who resembles the sun, whose entire form is white; through two years, she [attains] the state of possessing the nine jewels and other such qualities.
One should visualize three spokes in the form of a bow at the base of the penis, within the blood-vessel of the flavor [nāḍī],
appearing like the hollow of a *pārijāta* tree. Within that, one should contemplate the all-pervading *Kuṇḍalī*, who dwells in the apertures.
O Śivā, she who stands above the white, solar, and red mandalas, and who carries the moon—
may she speak these words to me during the fertile season so that my speech does not falter,
for you, O Auspicious One, know all the scriptures, traditions, lineages, and worldly sayings.
By the yoga of bringing about one's own year, the practitioner shall obtain the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
Through the three samās of Śambhu, he will certainly become an enjoyer of the qualities.
This is stated in the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya* leaf, which bestows the attainment of the five groups.
The meditation on the glorious Vaibhava has been completed; now, O tranquil one, [attain] the divine accomplishments (*siddhis*). The Seventh Section.
The silent practitioner should listen to the Śākta [teaching], which bestows many diverse accomplishments.
Meditation bestows immortality and likewise grants primordial knowledge;
it is the power residing within the center of the wheel of letters, which brings about the satisfaction of the body and so forth.
O Śivā, you are the giver of the nectar of omniscience from the ocean of firm beauty;
you are the Power (Śakti) born from the Moon-drop and the Sound (Nāda) through the movement of the breath;
you move within the cavities of the heart, throat, and the golden lotus of the head.
The sequence of the stages of arising from the mantra consisting of the letters [expressing] the self, the senses, and the void;
Śakti is the single breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and by that, the measure (mātrā) is declared by Śiva.
Through measures numbering one hundred, the penetration (āveśa) pertaining to knowledge shall occur.
The *śakti* is like an immortal elephant; it destroys grey hair.
Having brought about [the union] between the emission (*prasūti*) and the drinking (*pāna*), make the womb firm therein.
Then, contracting the *śakti* like a wheel, burn [it] by means of the sequence.
Having meditated thus, one should sequentially pierce the [centers of] pleasure and the rest with the Holder of the Wheel (cakrin);
having split them, one should enter the end of the cavity, which is the locus of the thousand-spoked lotus.
That mandala, the support of the *suṣumnā*, is pierced by the touch of its power.
Instantly melting, he becomes the destroyer of wrinkles and grey hair, like the orb of the moon.
Then he should pierce the root of the nose (ghoṇinī-mūla) and the [centers] beginning with Vāgīśvarī.
At the end of that, the life-force (jīva) falls within the feet; such is the continuity of those days.
Then, through the practice of leaping,
the decay of the body known as wrinkles and grey hair ceases entirely due to the attainment of equanimity;
for the person practicing this posture, qualities arise from the harmony of the constituents.
Having attained the quality of sovereign power, she did not leave her lord;
then, falling from one side with her body overturned— (p.
The lotus of gold, having come together and returned repeatedly just once,
joined with the previously mentioned numbers as before,
becomes the yogi of meditation and knowledge through a twofold repetition by means of the ninefold self.
One should meditate upon that transformation of the mantra, emerging from the interior of the cave with a vibration like a lotus fiber in a mire of blood, tearing open the gateway to the heart.
By this, within a year, one is born possessing qualities superior even to the lords of poets.
Within three years, one who possesses qualities equal to those of Śambhu shall meditate upon that lamp-like [form] encircled by the foremost of the Kṣatriyas and cows;
with his mind fixed on it, he attains the state of those whose nature is the cessation of breath.
When recited even once by those previously mentioned,
it produces possession (*āveśa*) regarding the meaning of the words, just as was previously described.
Therein occur trembling, laughter, rolling about, poetic inspiration, and the vision of fire.
Great waves, falling down, the sounds of "hā hā" and "huṃ," seeing from afar, hearing, touching, and the occurrence of news;
[these] arise correctly from the power of agitation.

When meditated upon by one whose eyes have been dissolved through contemplation, she who is endowed with fourteen powers and is devoid of the left-hand power (savya-śakti) causes all beings to melt away;
yet that same goddess, when meditated upon without the anusvāra, rains down the fruits [of one's desires].
Having recollected the spear of the serpent-eater (*garuḍa*), which destroys all suffering along with its emission (*visarga*),
one should discharge it at the Kṣatriya.
For the destruction of all afflictions during the body of one bitten and fallen asleep,
O Dear One, one should employ a slap, a sprout, water, oil, an ointment, and a staff;
by all these means, O Beloved, one should destroy [the poison] through the recollection of Brahmā, Prajāpati, and Śakti.
By the power of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣāvarta*), O child, one may destroy stationary objects and the like;
by the mere sight [of the deity], one gains poetic skill from Bṛhaspati through a good oblation;
and by the power of seven hundred thousand recitations, one attains the Śakti residing at the entrance of a cave.
In gold, it becomes the central essence even when devoid of mechanical processing;
in mercury, touch, poison, and scripture, it brings about immortality for the body;
and in procreation, enjoyment, and liberation, this single power bestows the entire world.

In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, in the chapter [dealing with] the attainment of the five groups, the divine meditation on Śakti has been presented; may you possess the divine accomplishments (*siddhis*). The Eighth Section.
One should meditate on one's own form situated within the center of the Leader’s belly—the stainless abode of eternal time—for the sake of supernatural powers; this destroys wrinkles and grey hair.
One should then contemplate that very form within the lotus of one's own body as oceans of nectar.
One should satisfy the true nature of reality for the sake of attaining firmness of the physical body.
By encircling [the body] from below the lotus-seated one and from above one's own lotus,
through the flowing of cool nectar during the three seasons, one becomes free from old age and death.
These two syllables, *sa* and *va*, are the seeds of the eyes;
through meditation upon them for three years, a person who has attained the sky is revealed.
One should meditate on the body itself as being submerged head-downwards within the Milk Ocean;
by doing so for a year, the decline of wrinkles and grey hair occurs.
One should meditate on the body standing upright, with the city of the head and the Dhṛtarāṣṭra mountains [the nasal bones] above it.
One should meditate upon the form of Śiva, which resembles the moon, for half a year, to destroy wrinkles and grey hair.
The yogi should meditate for half a year upon his own true nature, which shines like a celestial being and is endowed with stainless nectar, thereby destroying wrinkles and grey hair.
In the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), in sexual union (*surata*), in suffering, in happiness, and in the destruction of poison—
he who thus contemplates that Supreme One within himself and within his own heart,
[perceives] the Self through the conjunction of the three seasons situated within the ocean of milk.
The destruction of wrinkles and gray hair occurs, and one becomes happy among all beings.
O Goddess, liberation (kaivalya) may be attained, and through desire, there shall be invincibility;
there is separation from all suffering in that supreme, tranquil happiness.
The destruction of all poisons occurs through meditation within six months;
the attainment of omniscience within three years; and the radiance of the nine [planets] within nine years.
That which is acquired by Hara arises from the conjunction of five lines.
Having placed [the mind] upon gold, one should meditate on the Mother who has the luster of a creator;
this is declared to be the meditation on Brahman through the method of the *ajapā* [mantra].
By the turning back of the movement through the apertures, one reaches the further shore of disease.
The abandonment of Brahmā, poetic skill, equality with the earth,
and the power of moving through the sky shall come to pass in Durgā after three, two, two, and twelve hundred [years] from Śiva.
This is the supreme Brahman-sacrifice, which illuminates the Śabda-Brahman. It should be a fusion of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) and ritual worship (arcā).
Within the Supreme Brahman, which is utterly void yet blissful and rejoicing in bliss, [the sacrifice is performed].
Just as the two [shadows] vanish into the new sun at sunset, so the Lord of Yogis attains dissolution;
having first assumed a comfortable posture,
he should conquer the movement of the breath through the path of the nose and the crest-lock, and within six months, he shall become a destroyer of the king of bees (the vital breath).
Within three years, the state of omniscience is attained; within one year, one becomes radiant with the nine [powers].
This arises from the recitation of the mantra through repetition, without requiring any other moment of time.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, it is described as that which bestows the attainment of the five groups on the leaf.
May the meditation of Aindava be attained; may you possess the divine perfections (*divyasiddhi*).
[End of] the ninth section.
The reflection has the luster of gold, situated between two bows.
The ascetic, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), should meditate upon the fire together with Rudra.
Within one month, a pair of diseases is destroyed; within three and a half months, vision is restored;
within three years, he attains the state of Brahmāṇḍaga; and thereafter, he possesses the form of Acyuta.
If one is self-controlled, through the cultivation of the sun [meditation], after twelve years one becomes like the moon in luster and possesses the radiance of the sun;
this occurs with certainty.

One should meditate upon the fire of the great forest conflagration, whose source is the sacrificial hearth and whose rays are the qualities (*guṇa*), by means of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) within the practitioner; after a year, the Command (*ājñā*) proceeds.
At its conclusion, the desired movement of the two paths, characterized by coming and going, occurs for the sake of liberation.

Through the descent of all the gods, through the pilgrimage, and through the knowledge of lineage and non-lineage, all this proceeds by the power of the command of the practitioner. O Goddess, one becomes omniscient after twelve years, possessing the radiance of the sun.
One should meditate upon that reflection as containing consciousness while practicing breath-retention (*prāṇadhāraṇa*).

By doing so for one year, the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair occurs; by three years, one becomes like a god. And by means of that [practice], one who has descended from heaven, being pervaded by it, becomes similar to it.
By meditating for three years, one attains the Rājasa realm; hear now its qualities.
One should meditate upon the solar mandala as a seed-vessel situated within the reflection, pervading all directions and intermediate points, and encompassed by the forest of the [five] elements.
Within three years, there shall be the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair, and one becomes a Lord of Speech;
having become equal to the Omniscient One, one shall traverse the sky in that very body.
[The mantra] consists of the end of the end, joined with the sixteenth moon, the sun, the resonance (nāda), and the fourteenth.
One should perceive Śiva entering the city from the city of Jātarūpa.
He is like water in the mud of a buffalo, like fire in the desert, and like the sun in the sky;
he would certainly become equal to the fierce radiance of the wind’s speed.
For the sake of expressing the measure of the *puḥ*, there is the gentle recitation (*lāpana*).
One should worship the previously mentioned meditation on the *bindu* ten thousand times for its full resonance.
O Īśānī, until the end of the *nāda*, which is joined with a thousand suns,

one attains omniscience within three years and shall dwell directly in the city of Śiva. It is as vast as the sky at the horizon, like an autumnal cloud, and measured by the mere width of its own line.
Meditating upon Śiva, who is free from all limbs and devoid of objective domains,
one becomes endowed with spiritual realizations after three years and attains liberation while living;
like a staff or a wheel in the sky, one is not smeared by great defects.
This is the Śrīśāmbhava reality, which is devoid of individualized parts, eternally free from the triad beginning with *sadāśiva*, consisting of ultimate experience,
devoid of intermediate and final experiences, imperishable, and of the nature of fearlessness.
The meditation that is entirely nameless, which shatters all suffering without exception,
and which bestows the attainment of the five groups [of powers] according to the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*— may those divine perfections be yours, once that [meditation] has been mastered.
Tenth Section:
If he were to employ the means of subduing the forest-dwelling bhūtas and piśācas,
how could he then remove obstacles caused by the gods?
O Mṛḍānī, listen to this secret [teaching], which destroys great obstacles and accomplishes the purpose of mantra, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The two hundred and fifty mantras of Ālikāli were fashioned by Śambhu for the sake of human accomplishment through the power of mantra and for the liberation while living. These [mantras] of yours,
which follow the course of the Vedas, are the supreme vital points of the person.
These have been taught for the purpose of protecting the body and for the sake of attaining the five groups [of yogic powers].
When these are protected by the sixty-four *kūṭas*,
all obstacles to the arising of the body are destroyed.

All the *sakalā*, *sakalākalā*, *kalāniṣkalā*, and *niṣkalā* [forms] are prescribed for the protection of the body. Among those three types mentioned, the one called the *bīja* is the most excellent. O Dear One, whatever states of being are attached to this *bīja*-named ritual placement (*nyāsa*), [they are as follows]: * **Sakalā**: The state where all the limbs (*kalā*) are complete. * **Sakalākalā**: The state where some limbs are complete and others are incomplete. * **Kalāniṣkalā**: The state where the limbs are partially present and partially absent. * **Niṣkalā**: The state entirely devoid of limbs. Regarding these, the *bīja* is the best for protecting the physical form. O Beloved, whatever destinies are linked to this *bīja*-named placement, they are [described here].
They dwell among radiant beings, enjoying their respective groups;
by their own will, their noble means of accomplishment are always successful.
[These include] those that bestow the groups [of mantras], pertaining to the heavens, the atmosphere, and the earth.
An embodied being who has become liquid through the deposition of the seed-syllables cannot be slain by gods or other beings,
even with a glance, nor can they be seen by one possessed by anger.
If destruction does not occur for the performer of the deposition merely by the falling of a glance that perceives faults, [then it shall be so].
One should cause those wicked foods that create obstacles for beings to be distributed among their groups.
O Śivā, those accomplishments which are not achieved by a practitioner would not exist in this world;
therefore, a practitioner who is engaged in the ritual practice [should strive] for six months.
Having performed the ritual action in whatever manner [is appropriate], one will certainly become liberated while living.
When the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed for the solar year, the practitioner becomes a preeminent master of the means (*sādhana*).

O Goddess, by means of another creation from the Gītā, one may liberate or bind intensely; one may cause the dissolution of the individual soul into absolute liberation, and one may make even the Lord of the Earth a sovereign.
Just as Śambhu, Vidhi, Viṣṇu, Śakra, Mihira, and Soma [attain their respective states].

Likewise, by abiding in the perfection of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one dwells in heaven, enjoying its pleasures. All meditation, recitation, pilgrimage, fire-offerings, ritual manuals, worship, and so forth— indeed,
all philosophical systems— become the ritual placement within the seed-syllable until the supreme accomplishments are attained.

O Girīśānī, by means of a single utterance, one should accomplish the circle of the Sādhīnas through the deposition of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*) and the speech that expands the three commands (*tryājñā*).
Parā, with the oscillations of the four-faced one, [places] the moon-like [light] in the cavity (*bila*).
One should behold the collection of conditions for inspiration with a mind free from illness, like a flower in a vase,
amidst the moving and wandering of the boat, which is like the vital points of a spreading poisonous serpent;
it has a luster equal to the rays of a crimson mountain and is the remover of all sins.
O Dear One, at the base of the *liṅga*, [the deity] Vipatsomeśvara, together with Krodhaparāmbā, [pierces] the vital points (*marman*) of the anus with terrible fires. It is red-hued, O Beloved,
joined within Parāmbā with the excellent vital points of the *maṇḍalas* during the dissolution (*kṣaya*).
One should meditate on the semen (*śukra*) as *ka-ṣa-ra-pham* by means of the circles of the vital points (*marmas*) and so forth.
One should meditate on the blood (*rakta*) at the anus with the single vulva (*bhagāla*) of the camp of Śiva and Śakti.
Below the moonlight, one should meditate on that which has the luster of blood as Parāmbā by means of the sixth circle.
In the fat, red [is the deity] with the mind-born as the sixth; in the heart, Vidīśā is red.
[in] that cavity, at the opening of the anus, which has the marks of the vital points of the donkey, [he is] like gold.
One should destroy black [matter] with the feet of Garalāri, the circles, and the *ṇḍalas*.
One should lead away the blood from the vital points (*marman*) such as Dhabāśuga and others by means of the openings of the channels (*nāḍī*).
[This is done] by the lords of the serpents, the sixth, and the leaders of the biting ones, through the winds of bliss (*śarma-śvasana*).
For the lords of consciousness, one should visualize [the deity] as red through the assembly of powers;
[one should visualize him] as black with the final, intermediate, and root mantras in the right foot and the great toe.
With Śikhi, Soma, Āli, and Śeṣa, it is white at the throat and worshipped by the gods;
with Śakti, Īśa, and Anāla, it is yellow in the cavity;
with Khara, Marma, and Āla, it resembles gold in the anal opening.
One should destroy the black [element] with the six circles at the feet of the enemy of poison (*viṣṇu*);
the blood [element] with the vital points (*marman*) beginning with the white arrow (*vāyu*) at the cavity of the navel;
and the well-being (*śarma*) with the breath (*vāyu*), the lord of serpents (*śeṣa*), the sixth, and the fourteenth eyes.
The red [portion] is with the wood called *candrikā*; gold is at the anus.
Gold is at the anus; it is white at the tip of the crest with the supreme missiles of the Lord of Lust (*surateśa*);
it is white at the base of the crest with the nectar-juices of the Four-Faced One (*caturāsya*), O Beloved.
The mind is dark in its dissolution through the mandalas of the power of the earth of anger;
it has the ruddy luster of a banner through the three mandalas of the Great Yoni;
and it is illuminated within the cavities by the mandalas of the forest of Kaivalya-damana.
One should worship the white tuft of hair at the crown of the head with the *duḥkheda*, *daṇḍaśūka*, and *īśasena* [mantras];
and the garland within the cavity of the head with the *śikhin*, *sarpa*, *jhaṇḍalaka*,
*parāpareśvara*, *ahiśa*, and *śakyalai* mantras as its beads.
In his heart, he bears the pure lotus-stalks of the forest of enemies, which are like frogs of the poison of suffering;
in his heart, he bears the terrifying, dark-blue *kuṇḍalinī* womb through circles of light;
and he wears a garland upon the soles of his feet through circles of the sounds "rāva" and "jhaṇṭa."

In the heart, it is adorned by circles of liquid, trembling, and supreme nectar that destroy the son of the Supreme Brahman and are as firm as the fire of a forest conflagration; in the sky [of the throat], by clusters of *vatsanābha* poison; and on the head, by white [lotuses]. Thus [is the *Śukla* (White) yoga].
Indeed, with their mouths red from the venom of serpents that slithered toward others, they vomited forth misery through circles of double-tongued snakes hissing at enemies.
O Lord of Bliss, one should worship the red [deity] in the womb, bounded by forest groves;
one should worship [the deity] in the form of a dense cloud at the arrival of the rains within the thousand-petaled lake.
In the temple of Kuṇḍalinī, one should worship the red [deity] with the lotus-stalks of the serpent of Rati’s Lord.

The pair of hoods of the hissing serpent was like a circle of blood upon its face; the trunk of the headless torso (kabandha) was smeared with half-eaten flesh from the wheel-turner (cakrin); the blood flowed into the nostrils and the mouth;
and through the world-piercing apertures, it took on a crimson luster as it entered the openings of the veins.
In the skull-cavity (*kapālinī*) situated between the intake of breath (*prāṇa*) and the food of the Vedas (*śrutikāra*),
resembling a mass within the pleasure-grove of the worlds' bliss;
white with the twenty-four parts of the year beginning with the *mātrā*, it resides in the aperture of the head.
On the surface [of the wheel], it is free from weapons, consisting of the [triangles] of Aries, Peacock, Wind, Wheel, and Power;
on the level of the flame-tip, it is pure along with the circles of the worlds, rotating through the four faces of the mouth by means of the fire of the enemy-destroying lamps.
In the Śauklikeya [yantra], Harāmbā indeed resides in the mouth with the six, five, four, and three [syllables];
in the heart, she resides with the six, three, three, one, and two [syllables].
[She is worshipped] with the Tortoise, Mountain, Aja, Īśāna, Serpent, Śakti, and Surālaya [mudrās].
In the lotus-abode of Kuṇḍalinī, there is the appearance of fresh dūrvā grass sprouts;
with the essence of the Vedas in his mouth,
and together with the subtle particles of the Vedas and the fruits of the *rasāla* tree upon the knot of the Self-born One, he is dark blue.
White at the neck with the extremities of his serpent-ornaments, which resembled the moon and the sky,
he appeared like a stone on the eastern mountain, having assumed a form with fixed strides.
In the house of Ghoṇinī, there is a cloud of stainless water [offered] by Parā, Hālāhala, Arāti, Śakti, Soma, Āryamā, and others; likewise,
[there is water offered] with the juices of the five-fold end-maker (Pañcāntaka), Parā, Kāla, Raktameṣa, and Dharā.
Adorned by those who wear garments of darkness, the world— shining like the rising sun within the abode of the five senses,
possessing firm luster, harsh touch, sound, and delightful flavors,
and appearing as the manifestation of the subtle digits of fluidity— is indeed beautified by them.
In the presence of the Lord of the Goddess who wields the serpent-weapon,
with coral-like [limbs], there was within the two bows a sound like the heart of a *jhaṇṭana* bird;
indeed, the space between the two ends of the bow was filled in the heart by sixty-four *tālas*.
Adorned with the sounds *ra*, *va*, *repha*, *yoni*, and *alaka* at the upper opening of the navel-cavity,
it is auspicious like a serpent protecting the end-time; resonant with the sounds of the sky,
resembling an autumnal cloud, it resides in the primary chamber of all dwellings.
In the abode of the animal-born, it is yellow with kālakūṭa, hiṅgu, śikhi, soma, īśvara, and abhraka; in the house of the drop (bindu), it has the luster of the sun with nāga,
guhya, ambara, varti, sarpa, and kanālaka.
On the wooden plank, there were leaves from *vatsanābhi*, *hālāhala*, and *rasāla* [poisons]; and in the hole,
there was white sandalwood (*sita*), which provides comfort through its six-fold circle of hoods,
and which destroys the poison of the bees that are the anger of those who follow the conduct of Śiva.
O Dear One, the world-generatrix known as the double-tongued Śakti is drunk [by the practitioner] within the heart-lotus by means of the circles of sounds beginning with Śakti, Soma,
and Ādi.
One should meditate upon the white Himālaya as the bestower of power,
extending as far as the touch of the moon and other celestial bodies, consisting of fifty lotus-like men of noble character,
together with their mandalas, white in color, and possessing a luster like that of the setting sun.
This is the deposition of the sixfold seed-syllables (*bīja-ṣoḍhā*), which bestows the heart of all consciousness.
One should perform the deposition four times a day—on the secret place, the heart, the mouth, and the aperture—in due order.
O Durgā, this is most secret; it must be well-guarded and performed with diligence.
One should cause [the disciple] to offer [the oblation] in due order to Śambhu, who is the giver of all and is attained through devotion.

In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, this is described as the leaf that bestows the attainment of the five groups. May the sixfold seed-syllables lead to accomplishment; may you possess the divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*).
The Eleventh Section:
These seeds have been proclaimed as the givers of seeds, fallen from the *kalās*,
for the attainment of all perfections by men who perform the ritual actions accordingly.
For those who have abandoned worldly rules, fish, oil, women, and falsehoods,

there is said to be a dwelling-place for the body consisting solely of the *nyāsa* (ritual placement). Within that [body] are the two cavities, the plowshare, and the two conchs, situated between them.
The space between the eyebrows, the palate, the one called the throat-bell, the two ear-cavities, and the blind-well;
the throbbing pair below the throat and the two coils that encircle it;
the pair of armpits, the navel, the anus, the two palates, and the hole of the penis.
The distinction of the root of the *liṅga* consists of the pair of testicles, the creator, and the thread; above the anus, the fruit, and the *dhvaja*, there is the pair of wheels (*cakrayāmala*).
Two [joints] below the *cakra*, two at the ankles, and likewise two pairs below the ankles;
the pair of feet at the gates of Yama, the two palates, and the *kaśeruka*;
the four known as the sides and elbows, and likewise the two wrists.

O beloved, the two shoulders, the two nipples, the two corners of the eyes, as well as the nose, the forehead, and the ring finger— these are declared to be the abodes of the vital points (*marmans*) for men who possess good fortune.
One should worship the ninefold Goddess Niṣkalā, the root of those who possess distinctions, the seizing of the vital points (*marmasthāna*), the *samaya*, and the sandals of the Guru;
having worshipped these four times a day from the seed-syllable within the body, one attains everything.
Of what nature is that Niṣkalā Bhagavatī, the Samayā of the Lord?
Let the five-fold Samayā, who is the Earth (Dharitrī), be described with effort. Listen to the Samayā, O you of good ears; she is proclaimed as "Devi" (the Goddess).
By virtue of whose worship there is the worship of all the deities of all philosophical systems;
this city is proclaimed as the Great Yoni (Mahāyoni), pervaded by Hara.
The Goddess is the second, and from the mandala arises the second, the Cow-Milker (Godhnu).
Except for Moṭī, who is joined with Guhya, as well as Guṇaśambara;
Sparśādhyakṣa is joined with Leśa, and Nārāyaṇī is likewise.
Between these two, one should place Parva; these two constitute the half-van (vanārdhaka).
The *dharābaka* consists of two [fingers] reaching toward the throat, with the little finger and thumb touching the lips;
the *durbalā* pair embraces the neck at the vulva.
O Goddess, this path of worldly existence— which ends in the sound of the final *kṣvelā*— has been proclaimed by the Rudras as the ten *niṣkalā* [mantras] for the *daśaśambaras*.
Whoever should recite this Goddess even once every morning a hundred times, [attains the goal].
He possesses his own form and enjoyment, like Rudra in the city of Nāraka;
for the attainment of all categories of existence, one should meditate upon her as being red and extremely emaciated,
bearing in her right hand the half-moon of Brahmā and in her left a trident.

O beloved, one should worship the blue goddess, who wears a garland of skulls, who has elephants for feet, who sits in the lotus posture, and who possesses a gross body for the sake of enjoyment, by means of the yoga of non-action (akriyā) in the cave of the heart, O Goddess praised by the world.
His many sins go to destruction and he becomes joyful. Merely by the recitation of this [mantra], even the hosts of divine beings tremble before the speech of Śambhu, which crushes all obstacles.
Whoever recites this one million times along with *sahom*, for him there are accomplishments (*siddhis*);
wives become like household slaves, obedient to his word.
He in whose throat this mantra, accompanied by a host of other mantras, resides—
He alone, worshipped as Śiva, exists upon the surface of the earth in human form.
By him, the gods who have arisen from the support of the *rasas* are certainly worshipped;
for by whomsoever she is honored, O Goddess of Gods, she is the partless (*niṣkalā*) one who is worshipped according to the *samaya*.
Just as the sky is without stain, so one is not defiled by sins;
whatever one may obtain in this world through recitation, meditation, and so forth, it is due to the failure to remember the *samaya*.

The yogi established in the future lineage of the Yugas, by means of the ninefold creative emanations, should make [the practice] endowed with bliss; for the limbs of consciousness belong to that which is dear to the Intellect (citi).
When the Intellect is remembered, the yogi is not defiled by the multitude of faults associated with women or the years.

In the seed-syllable placement (*bījanyāsa*) for this worship, that which was previously taught by the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) is for the attainment of all perfections and for the fruit of the vital breath (*jīva*). In the *Parṇa* chapter of the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, it bestows the acquisition of the five groups of letters.
The illustrious Śambara has departed with the Goddess; may you possess divine accomplishments.
Thus ends the twelfth section.
This rite, when performed according to the form of the Guru, becomes successful.
Therefore, I shall speak of the worship of the Guru; listen, for it bestows spiritual perfection (*siddhi*).

When the planets Mars and Jupiter are situated in the portions of the Moon and the Sun respectively, one should worship the two supreme feet—the "Kakhe" and the "Phalamukha"—which are the gateways to the fruit and the movements of the lunar nodes (*parva*).
One should personally behold the world situated within the enclosure of those [deities].
One should offer a flower to the mortal [disciple] until the completion of the life-force (*jīva*).
With fresh [offerings], one should worship the Moon and Aruṇa three times each with ten [mantras].
At the conclusion of the sprinkling with the *kāraṇa* [mantra], one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) with the *devahṛdaya* [mantra].
At the end of that, one should worship the feet of the Guru with devotion in a manner similar to that [preceding rite].
O Dear One, for the sake of attaining the perfection of the [human] being, one should perform the threefold dissolution above the cavity (bilopari).
This is done by means of the one named Śivānanda, together with Śakti and Parāmbā,
within the enclosure of the primordial atoms at the beginning and the end, through their expansions, O Dear One.

Then, having meditated upon the Guru, whether he be manifest, born of the mind, or represented by written letters, one should perform the threefold prostration with the hands, the discus, and the palms. Worship performed without the discus is in vain; likewise, the recitation of Hari’s name is fruitless without the hands.
Without [the teacher's] word, there is the loss of everything, even unto death.
Thus, devotion, which is the limb of the means, should be directed toward the one who possesses the abode of the manifold and the uneven;
one should offer salutation to the superior essence for the sake of attaining the fivefold group.
One should wander alone upon the surface of the earth for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of bliss.
O Noble One, that which destroys all obstacles is the prop of a true friend;
one should recite it a hundred times with devotion, while meditating, prior to eating.
On the sacred day (parvan), one should offer an oblation (bali) to the sacred field consisting of a burnt fish;
however, excluding the Vaisāriṇa fish, one may offer the oblation with whatever items used for one's own nourishment.
By offering these substances on a Thursday, the ascetic shall thereafter become happy.

If [the rite] is easily accomplished, one should proceed afterwards; if it is at Puṣkara, one should proceed from the front. In the accomplishment of the hosts of spirits, one will certainly destroy obstacles.
Listen, Noble Lady, to that Śambara-mantra which visibly destroys obstacles.
Śambhu, accompanied by the anusvāra, is [formed] with the nāgas, the śaktis, and the three maṇḍalas;
furthermore, the outermost three maṇḍalas are drenched with the essence of great bliss.
O Goddess, you are the Veda-faced one, covered by a pair of swords, adorned with the earth and the Yuga;
you are the single one consisting of Time, the five elements, and the void, the double-egg, and the one worshipped by Bhauka.
You are the serpent, O Goddess, the pair of Yugas, the Veda-faced one, and furthermore, the bestower of bliss.
The pair of Pālīs, the two circles of time, the Sun, and the Lord of the Gods;
Rodana, the pair, is proclaimed by those who bear the hymns.
One born in Āṣāḍha is a Nāga; one should recite the final pair again.
O wise woman, these two mantras belong to the Leader Śociṣkeśa.
The twenty-four-syllable mantra is known as the field, and that which follows is the practitioner.
[They are for] those whose conduct is pure practice and whose selves are properly honored by the guru.
The northern direction is for the practitioner himself; there is no one else who might accomplish it.
Because it is easily accomplished in places such as a grove or a forest, one should cast the ninth [mandala] born of the earth.
This is the commitment (samaya) of the practice itself, performed first in the eastern mandala with the root mantra.
Once the maṇḍala has been completed, one should worship it thoroughly and offer an oblation accompanied by incense.
Thereafter, one should cause the ritual practice to be performed at the sacred site (tīrtha), for it is there that the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is prescribed;
and by that command, even minor success (siddhi) is attained by men.

In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya* chapter, which bestows the attainment of the five groups, the extraction of the Goddess’s garment has been completed; may your perfections be attained. The thirteenth section.
O All-pervading One, I shall state the minor means for those belonging to the various classes—
those born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes— who perform excellent sacrifices.
People will for the most part have minds intent on power and enjoyment;
they will be averse to *nirvāṇa*, desiring instead the path of worldly rebirth.
[They will be honored] by the sun, moon, fire, and the powers of the serpent-king and the celestial umbrella of the gods.
In this way, O Goddess, one should mutter five hundred [times] daily at the feet of the Goddess the syllables of Kamalā, which grant the fortune of a crane,
for half a year plus twenty days.
Facing the east, one should offer ten thousand oblations of milk— mixed with the essence of the *manaḥśakti* plant— into a circular fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) filled with flowers;
or else, facing the east, one may offer the grains of the *śāṇḍilya* plant.
One should always offer oblations with milk, remaining constantly devoted to daily ablutions.
One should observe celibacy, remain silent, and avoid the speech of a sovereign.
O Dear One, one should accomplish the lotus-like saliva situated within the blue boar.
The King of Yakṣas, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, [attains his status] by means of a sixtieth part [of that merit].
Truly, the speech concerning Maheśvara was proclaimed to you by the Great Serpent.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, this is found in the chapter that bestows the attainment of the five groups.
The divine Śrīsādhana is completed; may you possess divine accomplishments.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.
It is appropriate for householders to seek protection from the king against those who are deformed; however, one should bring about the pacification of the virtuous. Tell me the means for that.
Having diligently worshipped the Goddess Samayā, who dwells within the pavilion, [one should proceed].
By means of the excellent causes of parched grain, flowers, incense, ointment, lamps,
and unbroken rice, on a pure day, one should draw there upon a clean cloth— preferably that of Sindh— this beloved wheel which bestows all desires, according to the traditional injunctions.
One should draw the protective diagram (*saṃvarttikā*) for the seeds of *bimba*, *śāli* rice, and *māna* using the juices of *kīra*,
*candana*, *āhlāda*, *taru*, and *roga*, along with water. Having offered gifts to the *dānavas* within a sphere of dates and a golden milky tree, one should proceed.
Just as the mantras follow their sequence from the image (bimba) up to the deities,
so too is the Goddess in the image, and [the offering] in the front vessel as appropriate.
In this very way, O Lord of Vasus, the subtle [reality] exists everywhere through the secret mandalas.

The letter *la* (alivarṇa), joined with the dot of Hara (*harabindu*), [is placed] within pavilions formed by lotus petals; one should place the letters of the mantra upon leaves that cover both hands. One should place the seed-syllables (*bīja*) among the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*) and divide the circle into three parts.
Then, O Pārvatī, one should wrap it with a single circular *sṛṇi* cord;
above that, having wrapped it with the *kuṇḍaleśinī*, one should install it.
Having placed that pill in the hand, O beloved, one should mutter the *śambhu* mantra.
The noble ones [hold her] by the neck, men by the hips,
kings by the arm, and those of the animal species always by the breast, O beloved.
For one who possesses fortitude, there shall be no vision of untimely death,
nor fear of water, fire, serpents, [pu]kkeśas, spirits, or vetālas.
Such a person is liberated from all diseases and freed from all obstacles.
O Goddess, beloved of the Lord, this is born of truth in the fearless state.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, this leaf bestows the attainment of the five groups;
may you possess the divine perfections that grant the cessation of all longing.
Fifteenth Section:
One should reflect upon the soul as both metaphysical and material, and then adopt the practice of gradual progression.
Furthermore, even at a sacred pilgrimage site, a person may perform their actions in whatever manner is appropriate.

Because the body is attached to sense objects, life does not possess the power of action; therefore, it does not perceive. For this reason, I shall describe to you the Śambara of the Āryā-entrance, which illuminates the past, the present, and the future.
The maiden, having entered the mandala and being honored by the practitioner,
has performed her ablutions with perfumes, incense, lamps, garments, and fragrances;
honored with divine flowers, she stands within the mandala facing the east.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] on the head a hundred times with the mantra using the left hand,
accompanied by flowers. Then, O Goddess, one should ask about one's own auspicious and inauspicious [fortune], just as the practice for attaining welfare is explained in a secluded place.
One should then resort to it, or perform the transference of consciousness, or seek union with the sacred sites;
having fully realized this, who indeed would not be happy?
For that purpose, having prepared the garment for her, the Supreme Self—
listen with a one-pointed mind, O virtuous lady,
to how that garment reveals the auspicious and inauspicious states residing in the minds of all people.
O Goddess, [the mantra] is not overcome by the three circles, nor by the two *jhaṇṭaka* syllables of the fifth [vowel];
it is honored by the mind and the ears, O Goddess, and encircled by the triple-staff and the fish.
It possesses a pair of lips like the earth-supporter (the mountain), and Kālī is accompanied by the *bhūta*s.
O Dear One, Nārāyaṇī is Pukvasinī, encircled by the womb.
Cokhākya is Kālasargī; this is declared to be the three-syllable [mantra].
The second [syllable], pervaded by the sixth vowel, is prescribed as the ritual for the hand-limbs.
O Dear One, having recited this one hundred thousand times at the tip of the Goddess’s spear and performed the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that amount,
one should thereafter perform the practice (*sādhana*) in the form of a youth.
O Goddess, this is most secret and produces immediate conviction.
One should perform the practice with faith for the sake of all conviction.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, this [text] bestows the attainment of the five groups on the leaf;
may the state of the Kumārikā have entered you, and may the divine siddhis be yours.
The Sixteenth Chapter.
116) The stages of the earth, water, wind, breath, self, and others do not exist [as independent entities].
As long as they are conquered only gradually, how can there be success?
When they are mastered through the sequence of worship, meditation, and recitation, then liberation— which bestows the light of life— shall arise for the person.

Liberation is proclaimed as absolute isolation (kaivalya); yet even that single state is described according to the qualities (guṇas) of the bound soul (paśu). These [other forms] have been mentioned, and the remaining ones are said to be fashioned by the bound soul.
The certain conviction regarding the body is that it must be separated from the person at the end of creation.

Bondage and liberation are declared to consist in the connection with the two types of karma. Through the cessation of the primary principle (pradhāna) from the process of creation, there is separation from the circles of embodied beings;
the abandonment of the two types of karma is called the liberation of the deceased.
Through the stability of the ninety-nine senses along with the spheres of the body,
one attains the state of *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living), which endures for immeasurable time.
There is no creation, no departure, and this world is neither empty nor its own realm.

"Neither I, nor you, nor that liberation— this is the state of a bound soul," thus the second [state] arises from the teaching of the Person whose nature is the Command, O Dear One. The third arises from the worship with devotion by one who is free from [attachment to] women and the like.
For those who are upright, simple, and whose bodies are unrefined—
even for animals— the primordial liberation arises within days.
Only for those whose dwelling shall be in the miserable realms [does it not occur].
For men who have endured the sufferings of incalculable time, the final [birth] arises;
this liberation, which bestows life upon those who uphold the Vedas, was proclaimed by Kaṇāda.
Now I shall speak of the means to liberation; listen to it from me.
The atoms of earth consist of four [qualities], those of water five, those of fire six, those of air seven, and those of ether eight.
Since the Śrutis are the supreme elements of the celestial realm,
O Goddess, their sequence consists of the Vasus and the Yugas, which bestows the attainment of the five groups.
Through the propitiation of these, O Goddess, the rays of the Supreme Śambhu [are attained].
They become gracious toward virtuous men, even while they possess the intellect for debate.
These [qualities] revolve within the bodies, the dwellings, the beautiful faces, the lotuses of the lords, and the moon-drops of those men who act for the sake of liberation while living.
The rays of the sun, white and darkened by the time of the palm-leaf [twilight], produce sounds in the form of squares,
octagons, hexagons, and circles respectively;
they possess firm brilliance, intense command, atomicity, and the knowledge of the course of all effects.
The states of those virtuous men who are liberated while living arise in due order;
they are designated by name as deities for the sake of attaining perfection and for the purpose of worship leading to liberation while living. Listen with a one-pointed mind, O virtuous lady.
Oḍḍaja, Ālapūrṇa, Kāmeśvara, and their Śaktis—these are the subjects to be designated;
thus the group of four is proclaimed.
[The lords] are named Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Śaṅkara, Piṅgala, and Sadyojāta.
The powers are considered to be the sky, sound, the mortal world, the netherworld, the serpents, water, and speech;
they originate from the series of blisses and are capable of transcending the stages.
Karālā, Kāsā, and Hapanī are considered to be the Śaktis residing in the Hrānta [cakra].
Ādhārī, Cakrī, Kuraṅgī, and Madandhrī constitute the group of four;
Raktā, Caṇḍā, Karālā, and Ucchuṣmā are his Śaktis.
Those known as Jñāna, Ṛṣi, Ratnapūrṇa, Siddha, Aśṛṅga, Anta,
Kamala, Ākula, Dīpa, Barbarāpāca,
Vṛddhika, Paraśambhu, Navaveśana, and Svasitāṅga are the Mitras.
For Riccā, Amata, Kākālī, and Kubjikā are considered to be the Śaktis;
likewise Pīṭha, Yoginī, Samaya, Siddha, Ratna, Jñāna, and Kā.
The final number of these is four, beginning with one, and they are the arrows of the [five] courses.
Furthermore, the third eye is at the tip of the nose between the eyebrows;
the second [eye] is on the chest, the two sides of the chest, the heart, and the throat;
the third [eye] should be on the cheeks, the two depressions, and the temples.
The fourth [deity] is Prāṇavāgīśī, located on the two cheeks and the arms;
the fifth is Candrikāmā, located between the forehead and the aperture (brahmarandhra) in the heart.
The deities Kucā, Cibukā, Karā, and Devā are the Puṣpakas, each occupying half a digit (ardhakalā).
One should worship with fragrant flowers produced in their respective seasons, along with incense and other offerings.
For the sake of enjoyment and liberation, one should worship the *aṇus* and all the *caturthikās* and *ṛkās*.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, it is stated that this [practice] yields the attainment of the five groups (*pañcavarga*) upon the leaf.
May your sequential worship be accomplished, and may the divine perfections be yours.
[End of] the seventeenth section.
The peaks of the eight elements of the world-father, known as the *bhūta*-gatis,
are declared to be the skies of the sequences, arranged in three groups of fortnights.
The five classes consist of the five seed-syllables of bliss, the supreme, the letter *ba*, and the five seed-syllables of *abbā*.
The dissolution [of the rays] occurs in the corners of the aesthetic flavors (*rasakoṇa*), and in the cavities such as the forehead (*phāla*) and so forth, respectively.

When the Father and Mother of the World are said to reside within the internal image (*antarbimba*), the Leader of the Rays (*raśmināyaka*) and Śiva are worshipped; their dissolution takes place in gold and other such auspicious materials.
O Umā, I shall explain in due order the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) that bestows the attainment of the [spiritual] classes (*varga*),
just as it was taught by the Great-minded One in the *Lakṣapāda* starting from the fourth chapter:
"By means of nine, a newborn flower, a *kīra*, and the moon, [the measure is] merely a *praṇi*."
Having formed a boundary all around, one should effect the destruction...
In the practice of the tradition (*āmnāya-sādhana*), those [deities] mentioned for the directions, the back, and so forth, are placed;
and in the center of the fourfold [array], there are nine.
Having worshipped the two deities, one should mutter those [mantras] five hundred times each.
For the sake of consecration, one should offer ten thousand yellow flowers soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhu*) into the fire;
at the conclusion, there shall be sovereignty and the body shall attain firmness.
Thus, one who possesses such qualities, whose mind is like nectar through hearing [the teachings], and who is freed from the two diseases of the body, shall attain liberation while living.

The worship of the fourfold [deity] is prescribed upon a pedestal, in the sequence of extraction (*samuddhāra*), in a ritual substance (*dravya*), in sandals (*pādukā*), in a *liṅga*, in water, on a donkey, and in an effigy (*pusta*).
[This occurs] above the hand of the Lord of Herbs (*Oṣadhiśa*), by means of the causes for the destruction of the deer.
Having drawn [the diagrams], one should perform the sacrifice for those two with five pairs and two hundred [repetitions].
Immediately after that offering, one should recite the mantra for five hundred and fifty pairs.
Having given this, the mortal shall become happy as long as the moon-marked stars endure.
O Supreme Goddess, one who is free from wrinkles and grey hair, and joined by nine thousand elephants,
should worship this [mantra] for the awakening to all scriptures;
after three years, he becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and shall dwell in the space above the ears.
One should worship the two lotus-feet, which have been placed within the cavities of the heads of all the immortals,
upon the bull and the elephant, smeared with yellow sandalwood paste,
using black flowers; [one should also worship] the Supreme Lord and his consort in their midst.
Having recited it three hundred times multiplied by three (nine hundred times), O dear one, he who desires wealth shall accomplish vast siddhis, just as I shall describe to you:
he becomes uncuttable by any weapons and impenetrable by any missiles.

Inconceivable by all consciousnesses, which are associated with diverse objects, one should prepare an altar there above using fragrant cow dung, saffron, and sandalwood as the materials; having done so, one should worship Śruti with sacrificial pits.

Having attained the aforementioned qualities at the end of that [time], by means of those which resemble jars blackened by time and which are fourfold as previously described, he reaches the city of Vāyu.
