O beautiful one, having prepared a reflection with *arjuna* materials and the upper mandalas through conscious awareness,
one should worship the pentad by means of a fivefold recitation.
Having established all qualities beginning with earth, [one should proceed] by offering oblations into the ether.
Having become a knower of all, one should sport; and thereafter, one should proceed to the Supreme.
With pure, unadulterated devotion, one should offer the end [of the thread] upon the formidable, staff-like summit; through this sixfold devotion, the supreme goal is attained.
This most secret practice has been proclaimed as the bestower of rays, O Supreme Goddess; it grants all nectar and bestows liberation while living.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, this leaf yields the attainment of the five groups.
May you possess the divine perfections that result from the worship of atoms.
[End of] the eighteenth section.
A true disciple is one who is intent on hearing [the teachings], yet does not grasp them correctly.
Listen, for the sake of inspiring confidence in your intellect, I shall say something:
that which is born with a wisdom capable of overcoming even a hundred teachers of the gods—
that leader of speech which instantly produces conviction.

O Lord of Sages, having performed the recitation while the sun is invisible and remaining established in the ritual of the Grandfather (Brahmā), one should accomplish the goal through the prescribed practice by reciting seven hundred thousand times.
Then, that atomic soul, accompanied by hundreds of lords of yogis, [attains success] at the beginning of the Sarvamedha and other sacrifices.
I shall describe that which consists of darkness and delusion, the end of suffering, and the single body.
[He is] Kuṇḍalī, the Lord of Kuṇḍalins, and the triad of Kuṇḍalins and Kuṇḍalīs.
In the abode of Kuṇḍalinī, one should worship the flickering [deity] surrounded by dancing flames.
This is the heart of the wise regarding both poison and sense-objects;
indeed, this is the true word of Maheśvara for everyone.
At the conclusion of the proof of the stated meaning, love for the *khara* (the letter 'kha') shall arise spontaneously.
He becomes a master of ten million words from the Lord of Speech (*Bṛhaspati*), equal to the Three-eyed Lord (*Śiva*) and the like,
a peer among all scriptures, and a proclaimer of all the *Āgamas*.
I shall be the author, joined with logic; it arises of its own accord.
O Goddess, the seat of the Vedas is not indeed a lotus by its color.
One should offer the seat of Hari, which rises upward from the *saṃvit* and is the sovereign of the supreme.
One should worship Sarasī, who resides upon the crest of that seat, who possesses a garland like a row of autumn clouds, who always bestows fearlessness and prosperity, and who has three eyes.
One should worship her limbs in two ways by means of the falling drops of the essence from its peak.
The heart is designated as the abode; it flows within the virtuous person when the vital breath (āśuga) moves therein.
For children and the very elderly, the elaboration of refined speech (*saṃskṛtagīḥ*) is [not required];
these [others] recite according to their desire, even by means of mere fragments or syllables.
Remembering the command of the illustrious Śāmbhavī and recollecting the words previously uttered, they speak with certainty waves of speech as numerous as grains of sand.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, this chapter—which bestows the attainment of the five groups—has been thoroughly understood by means of the intellect. May you possess divine accomplishments!
The nineteenth section.

O Lord, tell me that means by which one may attain safety even from those who have reached the speed of a thunderbolt or are fashioned like a mechanical engine; for there is no safety from them for anyone else. May the practitioners be filled with the Rudras, their minds intent upon the mantras of Rudra.
Whenever its manifestation may occur for one intent upon that means,
O Sage, listen to the warding off of those wicked ones who create obstacles and cause suffering— the cause of all spiritual accomplishments.
There is one destroyer of obstacles, the crest-jewel of the self-willed Śiva;
he is the sun of knowledge who opens the lotus-like faces of all the sons of Aditi.
Whatever supernatural power (siddhi) the best of men desire upon the surface of the earth—
They quickly attain that true spiritual power, free from all obstacles,
just as Śambhu is the new Īśāna born from the Aghora-samaya; for this Blessed One is composed of all splendor, both auspicious and inauspicious.
Wherever obstacles arise for the practitioner, there he should remember Śiva;
in each such place, the destruction of those obstacles is brought about.
He is the Lord of Bliss, the Sovereign of Delight, and the destroyer of the pearl-oyster.
This milk-rice (*pāyasa*), which is fixed upon the abode of the essence of the *pakṣa-āmnāya* and has its dwelling established in the *suparṇa*,
is praised as the crest-lock (*śikhā*) when there is an obstacle in the milk-rice.
The destruction of those obstacles is praised when the Jātavedas [fire] is extinguished within.

At the beginning and end, the Earth [element] resides in the earthen [state]; one should carry away the sound-Brahman (nādabrahma) as the tone. Through the union with internal movement, arising from the center, it destroys all obstacles.
One should gradually place Śiva within the golden cavity of one’s own heart-lotus;
by virtue of His leading the way, He enters the mouth of the lotus-born Brahmā.
He has nine faces, possesses nine limbs, and resembles a swift, small deer.
With his face slightly blood-stained and variegated on both the right and left sides,
he [stands] upon the sun and the half-moon of the guardian of the Ḍiṇḍika; with his two arms, he strikes Viṣṇu with weapons fallen from the corpse, while wielding a trident and a sword.
Seated upon a lotus throne on a lotus that is supreme to Brahmā and imperishable, joined with all the fierce [deities], and with his crest-tuft rising upward like the Lord of Crests (Śikhānātha)—
O Goddess, by reciting this three hundred thousand times, there is nothing that he cannot accomplish.

In the Rasa-śāsana, at the conclusion of every oblation, except in the event of an obstacle, one should remember the God; during an obstacle, one should offer half of one's own portion for the sake of one's own success. True indeed are the words of the Māheśvaras—what else do you ask?
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, on the leaf that bestows the attainment of the five groups,
may you possess the divine perfections (*divyasiddhi*) of the Lord of the Crest (*śikheśa*), whose goal has been reached.
The Twentieth Section.
Now, if it is not possible to perform [the rite] for the body of Bījaṣoḍhāśikheśvara,
then one should, according to the rule, place that moving wheel upon its [the deity's] locus.
The [mantra] named Umāmaheśvara bestows the fruit of all ritual installations (nyāsa);
by remembering it four times a day, all obstacles are destroyed.
[It represents] the Lord of the Cavity (Bila-nāyaka) belonging to Śambhu, which has its root above and branches below.
With its root below and branches above, vast and hanging in emptiness—
this attachment between these two within the body is praised for the attainment of all perfections;
it is likewise praised for the success in the encircling of the moon, the gateway, the Śrī-bindu, and the face.
The mind is the Kundalini residing in its own support, the gold for the creation of the universe.
This is the glorious Guha-nyāsa, the singular embodiment of all planetary influences.
Whoever performs this nyāsa, which bestows a multitude of attainments, three times a day, [attains the highest goal].
For the sake of destroying all obstacles, that very Lord, ever-new,
has himself [bestowed] the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya* leaf, which grants the attainment of the five groups;
may the venerable *tadgraha* arrangement be yours, and may you possess divine accomplishments.
The Twenty-first Chapter:
What is the means for the happiness of those who have begun [the practice], whose souls are solely devoted to the study of the scriptures,
yet who still harbor desires for the enjoyment of food and other such things?
Listen, O Goddess of Gods: there exists [a place] to the north of Kāmarājapura,
which causes the agitation of cities and bestows supreme bliss upon all.
For those men who have taken refuge in Kāmeśvara but whose intellects and minds are yet unripened in knowledge,
kingship arises before long through agitation. Having placed the devotee at their forefront, they regard life itself as a means for obtaining food.
One should perform the propitiation at the end and abandon the enjoyment of animal sacrifices.
In the morning, [he appears] as the Sun, tranquil, wearing a jewel crown,
rising above the lotus, three-faced, nine-eyed, and marked by a garland of blue lotuses.

Adorned with various jewels, garments, and ornaments, he sits upon the seat of Hari. He holds a vessel of nectar in his hand and is seated upon the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus formed by meditation.
He is joined by the eight Kāmeśvarīs and is seated on the throne of Kāmarati.
Wearing the *liṅga* upon his head, he causes agitation in all the worlds.
The God holds a bow and arrows, as well as a goad and a blue lotus.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, the God Kāmeśa is the bestower of arousal.
All these powers have the form of horses and reside within leaf-palaces;
they are the powers Rati, Pratidhvani, Śānti, Puṣṭi, Śrī, and Mati.
Above that is a four-cornered mandala with a door extending toward the west.
O Lord, all the gods situated in the center of the triangle hear the sound of the door;
O Lord of the Supreme Earth, having consecrated the faces and voices of the sky-clad ones through the sounds of the other beings,
they become masters of speech along with the Guhyakas.
The second [circle] should consist of the *pakṣa*, *ambikā*, *cara*, vital points (*marmāṇi*), forests (*vana*), and mandalas;
the third [circle], consisting of seventeen syllables all around, is the subtle Lord (*pati*).

Having recited one hundred thousand [mantras] before the fire, at the conclusion of the *homa* sacrifice, the Brāhmaṇas and others, as well as kings and so forth, and even celestial women, come under one's control;
the yogin himself is then sought after by the twice-born, the kings, and others.
The noble poet effortlessly attains each of those [goals].
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya* leaf, which bestows the attainment of the five groups (*pañcavarga*),
may the divine perfections (*divyasiddhi*) be yours, O protector of the city.
In the moon, the sun, the star Arundhatī, shadows, one's own form, and various transformations;
in deformities of the lifespan, the shadows of houses, the earth and other elements;
and in the deformities of dwellings, tremblings, and so forth.
Upon seeing beings with false views,
or during visions in dreams that appear equal [to waking reality] and are marked by the distortions of ill omens,
one should remember Mṛtyuñjaya with devotion; hear now how one shall become happy.
The seed-syllable born of Hiraṇyagarbha has the face of Hiraṇyagarbha;
it is joined with the two ends of the wings of Śiva’s face, ending in the unsmeared (aliptā) goddess.
Having thus recited it one hundred thousand times and performed a fire-oblation of one thousand [times], [one attains success].
His white form is eternally present in Mars, for he is the destroyer of death by the hundreds;
he wears the yogic mudrā, is peaceful, and is endowed with matted hair, the moon, and the three eyes.
The hand that holds another’s water-pot [the sun] rests upon a white lotus.
Even though death occurs after the five-fold affliction (*upaghāta*), it is conquered in due time;
for death born of a single cause does not produce calamities.

He who constantly employs water that has been consecrated a hundred times [attains] freedom from fear at all times, even for millions of eons. This is stated in the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya-parṇa*, which bestows the attainment of the five groups.
May the yoga that conquers death be yours, and may you possess divine perfections.
Now, since it is impossible for those addicted to sense objects to deceive the realm of the senses,
one who travels the path of sacred pilgrimage sites should proceed to the vicinity of the Bestower of Liberation.
In the absence of duality, knowledge then severs the bondage of the body through action and so forth;
having cut off the vital breaths at the mouth of the upward path (uccāra) and made it the way of liberation,
one should press the *lambikā*, the *vaktra*, the *kuñcī*, and the abode of impurity (*amalālaya*) for that purpose.

Then, with the head turned upward, one should remember the thousandfold power of fire. Having first performed the recitation with the "Siddha-pañcama-abhra-śruti-nāgara-savana-ālaka" [mantra], those who have mastered the practice are led by the winds into the cavity.

Possessing vital breath and sense faculties, they are the agents who bring about the withdrawal of the two types of karma; O Goddess, their instantaneous attainment is proclaimed as the supreme secret.
In the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, on the leaf that bestows the attainment of the five groups,
may you possess the divine perfections (*divyasiddhi*) such as the departure of the breath and success in the world beyond.
May all those who perform this entire work daily within the cave [attain them].
Without that,
O Goddess, perform for the sake of the fivefold creation what is external to the limbs of the Creator, having taken it into the limbs,
so that the body may attain youthfulness, as I shall explain to you.
Lokeśa, Keśava, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva,
and the rest of the series of lords are declared to be the essence of feces, urine, dust, and semen.
[They cause] the destruction of firm beauty, whiteness, the body, stability, and so forth.
If it is performed according to the prescribed rite, these [offerings] bestow their fruits in succession:
from milk-rice comes the foremost of gods, Yaja; his son is Hari himself;
Ādipuṣpa is Rudra himself; and Leja is the Lord (Īśa) accompanied by Umā.

O beloved, they provide one pala [of the substance] respectively for ointment, a drink, nasal drops, and food; now hear the distinctions between them. Having collected the essence of the preceding [ingredients] and processed it with earth and cloth—

Then, having rubbed the body for six months according to the prescribed method, one should administer nasal drops (*nasya*) along with the nails, followed by further rubbing. One should again administer the nasal drops for the attainment of the fruit of immortality like that of Aja.
Arishta, sesame, brahmī, vasuka, vṛddhadāraka,
śamī, kola, niśā, and vṛttā, enriched with human fat and oil.
By the practice of eating for six months, one attains the state of an immortal being;
O Dear One, immortality is attained in five months.
This is declared in the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya* as that which bestows the attainment of the five groups [of powers] upon the leaf.
The goal regarding the body has been accomplished; may you possess divine perfections (*divyasiddhi*).
The ritual service (*saparyā*) for a full year is attained through the offering of the thread (*sūtradāna*).
Just as the thread reaches the ninth aperture (*randhra*), so too is there the count of three hundred and sixty.
Nine finger-breadths on one side and adorned with nine knots—
one should thus tie the cord of the Samaya [initiate] with the root mantra.
One should offer it three times with the root mantra, and the dismissal should be performed with the heart mantra.
Having worshipped Damanaka with the limbs [of the mantra], one should worship it five times with the root mantra,
O Supreme Goddess, using the five limbs for the attainment of the monthly cycle.
Worship performed at the time of rising is double [the merit], and that performed at the time of lying down is fourfold.
One should perform the Guru-parvan according to the portion of the deceased or the living;
with the deceased [one says], "May the speech live," and with the living, "May it be dear.
Likewise, when the portion arrives, one should say, "May there be Bhairavas," and so for the twelve parvans.
Having offered the nine [offerings] beginning with Praṇava and the nine [deities] beginning with Mitra, the poet becomes purified on the festival day; the yogin becomes one whose essence is Śiva.

Having consecrated it one thousand times, [the preceptor], accompanied by well-performed oblations, should give a sprinkling with nine jars to a new manuscript, a child, or a cloth-painting that has been bathed with the five products of the cow,
for men who possess truthfulness.

One who has sprinkled [the site] a hundred times with the mantra of the Goddess consisting of nine syllables should perform the ritual observance at the sacred seats (pīṭha), fields (kṣetra), and the villages of the Siddhas.
Having tied [a cord] of five hundred [threads] upon a petal, he should wander across the surface of the beautiful earth.
I have obtained this essence consisting of one hundred thousand [verses], which bestows the [four] goals of human life.
O Dear One, the Lord of Thought (Matesha) consists of five hundred [verses]; one should keep it well concealed.
If a person of sinful mind should reveal this in the world in any way whatsoever, [he incurs great sin].
The noble ones take away his *piṇḍa*, which is the perfected attainment associated with the lineage.
O Goddess, for one who has been re-initiated and sprinkled in the teaching of *rasa*,
if [the teacher] should give [this *piṇḍa*] to him, there shall arise for him that perfection proclaimed in all the scriptures.

I cause [the lineage] to revolve: by Lakuleśin in the east, by Kroḍamuni in the south, and by Ciñcin, the seeker of the western goal, in the north. May the supreme Māheśvaras and the great Vaiṣṇavas [protect] that [lineage], O Maheśa!
"O Noble Lady, may they become tranquil; let the virtuous offer their discourse.
In the Śrīśambhunirṇaya-parṇa, which bestows the attainment of the five groups, the Śikhā-yoga has gone toward perfection; may you possess divine accomplishments."
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section. It is complete.
